![Thumbnail for Novara Media's *Downstream* episode with Karen Hao. [Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8enXRDlWguU).](cover.jpg){fig-align="center"}

In a June 2025 episode of Novara Media's *Downstream*, [Aaron Bastani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Bastani) interviews [Karen Hao](https://www.karenhao.com/) — the [MIT Technology Review](https://www.technologyreview.com/) and [Wall Street Journal](https://www.wsj.com/) reporter who covered [OpenAI](https://openai.com/) for years — about her book *Empire of AI*, built on more than 300 interviews, over 150 of them with current and former OpenAI staff. The conversation runs about 90 minutes and is less a tour of the technology than a structural argument: that a handful of AI labs are behaving like the old corporate empires, and that letting a small group concentrate this much power over data, energy, water, and labor is, in Hao's word, "structurally unsound."

A few takeaways, each linking to the supporting chapter below:

- [**"AI" is a suitcase word**](#ch-ai-explained) that hides enormous differences in scale and cost. Hao's analogy is "transportation," which can mean a bicycle or a rocket, and politicians who promise "more AI" rarely say which one they mean.
- [**The environmental bill is paid locally**](#ch-data-centres): data centers cool themselves with public drinking water and run largely on fossil power, so the cost lands on particular communities — a record drought in Montevideo, a housing-construction ban along the UK's M4 corridor.
- [**The race runs on ideology as much as economics**](#ch-major-players): with no clear business case, what sustains the spending is a genuine, quasi-religious belief that recreating human intelligence is the most important thing anyone could do.
- [**OpenAI began as an open nonprofit and inverted every founding commitment**](#ch-openai-rise) once it decided that scale, not talent, was the bottleneck. Converting to capture capital is what split Musk and Altman.
- [**Nobody could tell Hao what Sam Altman believes**](#ch-sam-altman): across 150 OpenAI interviews, the recurring account is that Altman reflects whatever the person in front of him believes — at once his fundraising gift and the root of his polarizing reputation.
- [**The supply chain looks colonial**](#ch-colonial): [Kenyan content moderators](#ch-global-south) and Venezuelan data labelers paid a few dollars an hour at one end, million-dollar pay packages and multi-trillion-dollar valuations at the other.
- [**Colossal scale is a choice the labs made**](#ch-deepseek): DeepSeek and Stable Diffusion reached frontier-level results with far less compute, undercutting the premise that giant data centers are required to build capable AI.
- [**The response is to contest the supply chain**](#ch-stop-big-tech): data, land, water, and the schools and offices where AI gets deployed are all publicly contestable, and Hao's optimism rests on people pushing back at every node.

With the help of AI, I've built an **[enriched transcript](#transcript) at the bottom of this post** — the YouTube auto-captions, content-diarized into speaker turns and sliced into the interview's chapters and finer topic subsections, with inline hyperlinks, acronym expansions, and editor's-note callouts. See the preamble of that section for what's verbatim and what's editorial.

### [0:03:11 — AI, deep learning, and machine learning explained](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8enXRDlWguU&t=191s) {#ch-ai-explained}

#### Why "AI" resists definition: a marketing term from 1956

**Aaron Bastani:** Yeah. Before we drill down into your book — what is AI, and what do people mean by AI when they talk about it in 2025 in Silicon Valley?

**Karen Hao:** This is — you would think this is the easiest question, but this is always the hardest question that I get, because artificial intelligence is quite poorly defined.

We'll go back first to 1956, because I feel like it helps understand a little bit about why it's so poorly defined today. The term was originally coined in 1956 by this [Dartmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmouth_workshop) professor, assistant professor [John McCarthy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McCarthy_(computer_scientist)). And he coined it to draw more attention and more money to research that he was originally doing under a different name.

And that was something he has explicitly said a few decades later. He said, "I invented the term artificial intelligence to get money for a summer study." And that marketing route to the phrase is part of why it's really difficult to pin down a specific definition today.

The other reason is because generally people say that AI refers to the concept of recreating human intelligence in computers. But we also don't have a scientific consensus around what human intelligence is. So quite literally, when people say AI, they're referring to an umbrella of all these different types of technologies that appear to simulate different human behaviors or human tasks.

But it really ranges from something like [Siri](https://www.apple.com/siri/) on your iPhone all the way to [ChatGPT](https://chatgpt.com/), which behind the scenes are actually really, really different ways of operating. They're totally different scales in terms of the consumption of the technologies. And of course they often have different use cases as well.

::: {.callout-note}
**Editor's note.** McCarthy's "get money for a summer study" line refers to the [1956 Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmouth_workshop), the workshop proposal — co-authored with Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester, and Claude Shannon — that coined the term. McCarthy was an assistant professor at Dartmouth at the time.
:::

**Aaron Bastani:** So right now, when OpenAI, Meta, when they use those words "AI" in regards to their products specifically — what are they talking about?

**Karen Hao:** Most often they are now talking about what are called [deep learning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_learning) systems. So these are systems that train on loads of data, and you have software that can statistically compute the patterns in that data, and then that model is used to make decisions, or generate text, or make predictions. So most modern-day AI systems built by companies like [Meta](https://about.meta.com/), by OpenAI, by Google are now these deep learning systems.

**Aaron Bastani:** So deep learning is the same as [machine learning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machine_learning) is the same as [neural networks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neural_network_(machine_learning))? These are synonyms?

**Karen Hao:** Deep learning is a subcategory of machine learning. Machine learning refers to a specific branch of AI where you build software that calculates patterns in data. Deep learning is when you're specifically using neural networks to calculate those patterns.

So — one of the founding fathers of AI used to call AI a "suitcase word." Because you can put whatever you want in the suitcase, and suddenly AI means something different.

So we have this suitcase word of AI, and then under that, any data-driven AI techniques are called machine learning, and then any neural-network data-driven techniques are called deep learning. So it's the smallest circle within this broader suitcase word.

**Aaron Bastani:** So deep learning and neural networks are kind of interchangeable.

**Karen Hao:** Not exactly, in the sense that neural networks are referring to a piece of software, and deep learning is referring to the process that the software is doing, right?

#### The "transportation" analogy: politicians who promise "more AI"

**Aaron Bastani:** Yeah. Do you get upset when politicians — so in this country we have a prime minister called [Keir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer), you know — and they say, "We think the NHS can save, you know, 20% by using AI applications"? Do you sort of think, "My goodness, these people have no idea what they're talking about," because that is such an expansive term? Its political convenience is precisely that it doesn't mean anything.

**Karen Hao:** It does frustrate me a little bit. I often use the analogy that AI is like the word "transportation." I mean, transportation can refer to bicycles, or rockets, or self-driving cars, or gas-guzzling trucks — they're all different modes of transportation, serve different purposes, different cost-benefit analyses.

And you would never have a politician say, "We need more transportation to mitigate climate change." You would be like, "But what kind of — what are you talking about?" Or, "We need more transportation to stimulate the economy."

There is a vagueness around the AI discussion that is really unproductive, and I think a lot of that leads to confusion where people think AI equals one thing, and AI equals progress, and so we should just have all of it.

But actually, if we were to use the transportation analogy — you know, having more bicycles, having more public transit, sounds great. But if someone were actually referring to just using rockets to commute from Dublin to London, and we were like, "Everyone should get a rocket now, that's going to bring us more progress," you'd be like, "What are you talking about?" And that's effectively what these companies are doing with general intelligence.

**Aaron Bastani:** When you're giving people tools for free with regards to generative AI to just generate stupid images of nonsense — that's kind of what we're doing, right? I presume you would take that analogy to that level. It's like saying, "Let's use a rocket to get from Dublin to London to Paris."

**Karen Hao:** Yeah, exactly. It's not fit for the task. And the extraordinary amount of environmental costs for flying that rocket, when you could have flown a much more efficient plane to do the same thing, is like — what are you doing?

And that's one of the things that people don't really realize about generative AI: the resource consumption required to develop these models, and also to use these models, is quite extraordinary. And oftentimes people are using them for tasks that could be achieved with highly efficient different AI techniques.

But because we use the sweeping term "AI" to mean anything, people just think, "Oh yeah, right, I'm just going to use ChatGPT for my one-stop-shop solution for anything AI-related."

### [0:09:27 — Data centres and resource consumption](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8enXRDlWguU&t=567s) {#ch-data-centres}

#### Projected energy demand: McKinsey's "half to 1.2 times the UK's annual consumption"

**Aaron Bastani:** So right now, data centers globally, I think, are about 3–3.5% of CO₂ emissions. The data centers for AI are a tiny fraction of that, but obviously they're growing at an extraordinary pace. Are there any numbers out there with regards to projected CO₂ emissions of data centers globally 5, 10, 15 years from now? Or is it so recent that we can't really speculate about the numbers involved?

::: {.callout-note}
**Editor's note.** Estimates vary by what's being counted. Data centers are usually put at roughly 1–1.5% of *global electricity use* (the IEA's figure for 2022 was about 1–1.3%, excluding crypto mining); the higher "2–4%" figures generally refer to the broader information-and-communications-technology sector, not data centers alone. Aaron's "3–3.5% of CO₂ emissions" is at the upper end of what's typically cited.
:::

**Karen Hao:** There are numbers around the energy consumption, which you could then use to try and project carbon emissions. There was a [McKinsey](https://www.mckinsey.com/) report that recently projected that, based on the current pace of data center and supercomputer expansion for the development and deployment of AI technologies, we would need to add around half to 1.2 times the amount of energy consumed in the UK annually to the global grid in the next 5 years.

**Aaron Bastani:** Wow.

**Karen Hao:** And most of that will be serviced by fossil fuels. This is something that [Sam Altman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Altman) actually even said in front of the Senate a couple of weeks ago. He said it will most probably be natural gas — so he picked the nicest fossil fuel.

But we're already seeing reports of coal plants having their lives extended. They were meant to be retired, but they're no longer being retired, explicitly to power data center development.

We're seeing reports of [Elon Musk's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elon_Musk) [xAI](https://x.ai/) — the giant supercomputer that he built called Colossus, in Memphis, Tennessee — it is being powered with around 35 unlicensed methane gas turbines that are pumping thousands of toxic air pollutants into that community.

So this data center acceleration is not just accelerating the climate crisis; it's also accelerating the public health crisis of people's ability to access clean air as well as clean water.

::: {.callout-note}
**Editor's note.** The Colossus turbine count traces to reporting by the [Southern Environmental Law Center](https://www.selc.org/), which used aerial imagery to count roughly 35 gas turbines at the Memphis site, many without the Clean Air Act permits the SELC argued were required. xAI has said it brought turbines on site to meet near-term power needs while grid capacity was built out.
:::

#### Fresh water for cooling, and the Montevideo drought

**Karen Hao:** One of the aspects that's really under-talked-about with this kind of AI development — the OpenAI version of AI development — is that these data centers need fresh water to cool, because if they used any other kind of water it would corrode the equipment, it would lead to bacterial growth. And so most often these data centers actually use public drinking water, because when they enter into a community, that is the infrastructure that's already laid to deliver fresh water to companies, to businesses, to residents.

One of the things that I highlight in my book is there are many communities that do not have sufficient drinking water even for people. I went to Montevideo, Uruguay, to speak with people about a historic level of drought they were experiencing, where the Montevideo government literally did not have enough water to put into the public drinking water supply. So they were mixing toxic waste water in, just so people could have something come out of their taps when they opened them.

And for people that were too poor to buy bottled water, that is what they were drinking. And women were having higher rates of miscarriages, elderly were having an exacerbation of their chronic diseases. And in the middle of that, Google proposed to build a data center that would use more drinking water.

**Aaron Bastani:** This is potable water, right? You can't use seawater, because of the saline aspect.

**Karen Hao:** Exactly. And Bloomberg recently had a story that said two-thirds of the data centers now being built for AI development are in fact going into water[-stressed areas].

::: {.callout-note}
**Editor's note.** The figure is from a December 2024 [Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/) investigation, which found that roughly two-thirds of new data centers built or in development since 2022 are in places with high water stress.
:::

#### "Unlicensed," and the erosion-of-democracy thesis

**Aaron Bastani:** You said a moment ago about xAI's unlicensed energy generation using methane gas. When you say "unlicensed," what do you mean?

**Karen Hao:** As in the company just decided to completely ignore existing environmental regulations when they installed those methane gas turbines. And this is actually one of the things that I concluded by the end of my reporting: not only are these companies really corporate empires, but also that if we allow them to be unfettered in their access to resources and unfettered in their expansion, they will ultimately erode democracy. That is the greatest threat of their behaviors.

And what xAI is doing is a perfect example, at the smallest level — these companies are entering into communities and completely hijacking existing laws, existing regulations, existing democratic processes to build the infrastructure for their expansion. And we're seeing this hijacking of the democratic process at every level, from the smallest local levels all the way to the international level.

**Aaron Bastani:** It's that orthodoxy of "seek permission after you do something" — when you start applying this, this is business as usual for those companies. That's part of their expansion strategy, which we'll talk about — and we're going to talk about the sort of global colonial aspect as well with regards to resource consumption, resource use.

### [0:14:30 — Who are the major players](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8enXRDlWguU&t=870s) {#ch-major-players}

#### The players: US labs, the Chinese ecosystem, and Europe's "tiddlers"

**Aaron Bastani:** Just to bring it back to the US again, because at the top of this conversation I want to offer a bit of a primer to people out there who maybe know what AI is, maybe have used ChatGPT — what are the major companies we're now talking about in this space, particularly in the United States, over the last 5 years?

Who are the people in this race to AGI — allegedly artificial general intelligence, something which either might be sentient (probably not) or capable of augmenting its own intelligence (more plausible)? Who are the major players in that field right now?

**Karen Hao:** One caveat on AGI is that it's as ill-defined as the term AI, so I like to think of it as just a rebranding. The entire history of AI has just been about rebranding, and the term "deep learning" was also a rebranding. So, anyway.

But the players: first, OpenAI, of course — they were the ones that fired the first shot with ChatGPT. [Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/), major competitor. Google, Meta, Microsoft — they're the older internet giants that are now also racing to deploy these technologies. [Safe Superintelligence](https://ssi.inc/), which spun out of OpenAI — there are many OpenAI splinters — this was founded very recently by the former chief scientist of OpenAI [[Ilya Sutskever](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilya_Sutskever)]. And [Thinking Machines Lab](https://thinkingmachines.ai/), founded very recently by a former chief technology officer of OpenAI.

And Amazon is now trying to get into the game as well, and Apple is also trying to get in the game. So basically all the older-generation tech giants, as well as a new crop of AI players, are all jostling in this space.

**Aaron Bastani:** And that's just the US, right?

**Karen Hao:** And that's just the US. The Chinese ecosystem is interesting, because they don't really use the term AGI. This is a very unique thing about the US ecosystem — that there's a quasi-religious fervor that underpins the construction of AI products and services, whereas in China it's much more like, these are businesses, we're building products that users are going to use.

So if you're just looking at companies building chatbots that are sort of akin to ChatGPT, then we're talking about [ByteDance](https://www.bytedance.com/), owner of TikTok; [Alibaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alibaba_Group), the equivalent of Amazon; [Baidu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baidu), the equivalent of Google; [Huawei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huawei), the equivalent of Apple; and [Tencent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tencent) — what is the equivalent of Tencent? I guess Meta is the equivalent of Tencent. So they're also building these things. And there's similarly a crop of startups moving into the generative AI space.

**Aaron Bastani:** And in Europe, we've got the little tiddlers, like [Mistral](https://mistral.ai/) in France — really not at the races, 'cause we're Europe.

What's the business case for all this? Because obviously you've got massive companies often driven by maximizing shareholder value, multi-trillion-dollar valuations. You do these things, you invest money to make money, as a capitalist society.

So what is the business case made by, say, Microsoft when they have their shareholder meetings and they say, "We're going to allocate $40, $50 billion towards building data centers"?

#### No clear business case — so what sustains it is ideology

**Karen Hao:** It's interesting that you mentioned Microsoft, because Microsoft has recently been pulling back their investments in data centers. They went all in, and now they're rapidly starting to abandon data center projects.

So to answer your question, it is really unclear what the business case is, and Microsoft has been one of the first companies to start acknowledging that. [Satya Nadella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satya_Nadella) has come onto some podcasts recently where he actually stunned some people in the industry by being quite skeptical of whether or not this race to AGI was productive.

But one of the things I really felt after reporting — what is driving the fervor — is you can't actually fully understand it as just a story about money. It has to also be understood as a story of ideology. Because in the absence of a business case, then you ask, why are people still doing this?

And the answer is, there are people who genuinely, fervently believe — and they talk about it as a belief — in this idea that we can fundamentally recreate human intelligence, and that if we can do that, there is no other more important thing in the world. Because how else should you be dedicating your time, other than to bring about this civilizationally transformative technology?

And so that's part of what drives OpenAI, what drives Anthropic, what drives Safe Superintelligence, these other smaller startups.

And then the bigger giants, which are more business-focused and more classic companies that actually care about their bottom lines, end up getting pressured, because shareholders are seeing the enormous amounts of investment by these startups, and they're seeing users start shifting from Google search to using ChatGPT as search.

ChatGPT should not be used as search, but consumers think that it is. And then shareholders ask, in Google's shareholder meetings, "What are you doing with AI? What is your AI strategy? Why aren't you investing in this technology?" And so then all of the other giants end up racing in the same direction.

::: {.callout-note}
**Editor's note.** The Microsoft pullback Hao refers to was reported in early 2025, when analysts at TD Cowen said Microsoft had canceled or deferred leases on some data center capacity. Microsoft characterized the moves as routine adjustments to its build-out and reaffirmed roughly $80 billion in planned fiscal-2025 data center spending.
:::

#### Thiel's monopoly orthodoxy, and the bubble risk to the wider economy

**Aaron Bastani:** What does Warren Buffett make of it? That's what I want to know. Is he sort of like, "You guys are wasting your money"?

**Karen Hao:** He's probably right. I have no idea.

**Aaron Bastani:** Has he invested in AI?

**Karen Hao:** No, I don't think so.

**Aaron Bastani:** He just sticks to Coke and these sorts of things, doesn't he. There's two rationales. One is, like you say, a quasi-religious fervor has inflected the investment decisions of some of the world's most valuable companies, which is just an extraordinary thing to even think about.

The other one is that a lot of people in this space, as we'll talk about in a moment, are heavily influenced by people like [Peter Thiel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Thiel). And Peter Thiel's orthodoxy is that competition is for idiots, right? If you're going to start a business, it has to be a monopoly.

And I can only presume that companies like Microsoft etc. — although maybe that's not the best example now, given recent events — but xAI, OpenAI, Meta, the only reason you would invest ultimately hundreds of billions, trillions of dollars into this, is because first-mover advantage gives you a monopoly on the most transformational technology since the steam engine. That's the only way I can make sense of it, right? Has anybody in that space kind of said that — "we want a monopoly on AGI, we want to be the Facebook of AGI"?

**Karen Hao:** Well, what OpenAI often says to investors is: if you make this seemingly fantastical bid into our technology, you could get the biggest returns you've ever seen in your life, because we will then be able to use your funding to get to AGI first. So it's still riding on this concept that there might be an AGI — which is not rooted in scientific evidence.

And even if we fail, we will successfully be able to automate a lot of human tasks, to the point where we can convince a lot of executives to hire our software instead of a labor force. So that in and of itself could potentially end up generating enough returns for you, more than you've ever seen before. So that's usually the pitch they make.

But it is a huge, risky bargain that these investors are pitching into. And a lot of investors have a bandwagon mentality — they aren't necessarily doing their own analysis. They're just seeing everyone glom onto this thing, and they're like, "Well, I don't want to miss out, why don't we glom on as well?"

But there are some investors that have actually recently reached out to me to be like, one of the most under-reported stories right now is the amount of risk that is being taken on — not just by these VCs [venture capitalists], it's actually being taken on by the entire economy. Because the money that these investors are investing comes from things like university endowments. So if the bubble pops, it doesn't just pop for Silicon Valley; it will have ripple effects across the global economy.

**Aaron Bastani:** When you look at the e-commerce bubble in the late '90s — okay, it was a bubble, you know, Pets.com or whatever, it had these crazy valuations — but buying and selling goods and services offline and then taking that online, I mean, that makes sense. That's a plausible commercial model. But like you say, nobody's really done that with artificial intelligence. It does kind of feel like — you read these stories about Tulip Mania in 17th-century Holland, and it does kind of feel very similar.

### [0:23:17 — What's behind OpenAI's rapid rise](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8enXRDlWguU&t=1397s) {#ch-openai-rise}

#### The founding: an open, anti-Google nonprofit

**Aaron Bastani:** You mentioned OpenAI, and we've talked about it many times — and of course OpenAI is the central organization in this book. What's the big idea behind OpenAI? When does it start?

**Karen Hao:** Let's see — end of 2015.

**Aaron Bastani:** 2015. So it's 10 years old. What are the animating values that give birth to OpenAI?

**Karen Hao:** OpenAI started as a nonprofit, which many people don't realize, given that it's one of the most capitalistic, if not the most capitalistic, organization in Silicon Valley today. But it was co-founded by Elon Musk and Sam Altman as a bid to create a fundamental AI research lab that could develop this transformative technology without any kind of commercial pressures.

So they positioned themselves as the anti-Silicon Valley, the anti-Google — because Google at the time was the main driver of AI development. They had developed a monopoly on some top AI research scientists, and Musk in particular had this great fear of not just Google but Google's [DeepMind](https://deepmind.google/) — Google's acquisition of DeepMind — where he was very worried that this consolidation of some of the brightest minds would lead to the development of AI that would go very badly wrong.

And what he meant by "very badly wrong" was, it could one day develop sentience, consciousness, go rogue, and kill all humans on the planet.

And because of that fear, Altman and Musk then thought, we need to do a nonprofit, not have these profit-driven incentives. We're going to focus on being completely open, transparent, and also collaborative — to the point of self-sacrificing if necessary. If another lab starts making faster progress than us on the quest to AGI, we will actually just join up with them. We will dissolve our own organization and join up with them. And that didn't hold for very long.

**Aaron Bastani:** So what's their theory behind that? Because at that point Google is maybe the world's most valuable company — I don't know, it's certainly up there — and this is a nonprofit. So how are they going to achieve AGI before Google?

#### Why a nonprofit? Mission as a recruiting tool

**Karen Hao:** So initially the bottleneck that they saw was talent. Google has this monopoly in talent; we need to chip away at that and get some of those Google researchers to come to us, and also start acquiring PhD students just coming out of uni.

And because of that, I have come to speculate — this is not based on any documents that I read or anything — I've come to speculate that part of the reason they started as a nonprofit in the first place is because it was a great recruitment tool for getting at that bottleneck. They could not compete on salaries with Google, but they could compete on a sense of mission.

And in fact, when Altman was recruiting the chief scientist, Ilya Sutskever — who was the critical first acquisition of talent, that then led to many other scientists being really interested in working for OpenAI — he appealed to Sutskever's sense of purpose: do you want a big salary and to just work for a for-profit company, or do you want to take a pay cut and do something big with your life?

And it was actually that reason that Sutskever said, "You know what, you're right, I do want to work for a nonprofit."

And so that's how they initially conceived of competing with Google: we're starting a little bit late to the game, how do we first get a bunch of really, really smart people to join us? Let's create this really big sense of mission.

#### "Build a religion": the 2013 Altman epigraph

**Karen Hao:** And I open the book with two quotes in the epigraph, and one of them is from Sam Altman writing a blog post in 2013. He quotes someone else that says, "Successful people build companies. More successful people build countries. The most successful people build religions."

And then he reflects on this and says, "It seems to me that the most successful founders in the world don't actually set off to build a company. They set off to build a religion. And it turns out building a company is the easiest way to do so."

**Aaron Bastani:** And so it's not like 2013, and then 2015 he creates OpenAI as a nonprofit. It's important to say as well, Sam Altman is not some sort of idealistic pauper — he's working at [Y Combinator](https://www.ycombinator.com/), he is very much enmeshed within the Silicon Valley elite.

I suppose also there's tax, right? If you're a nonprofit, you've got the mission, you've also got a bunch of tax breaks which you don't have as a for-profit. So maybe there's a very cynical genesis there.

But I suppose, just reading your book and becoming more familiar with the arguments over time — clearly the amount of compute you have was always going to be critical. And if you believe in the neural network model, the deep learning model, the amount of compute you have is always going to be critical. And it just seems implausible that a nonprofit could ever have been able to compete with Google. Because you have to spend, as we now see, tens of billions, hundreds of billions of dollars on compute.

Did nobody say that? Did nobody say, "Hey, the bottleneck isn't just talent acquisition, it's being able to spend hundreds of billions of dollars on these [Nvidia](https://www.nvidia.com/) GPUs [graphics processing units]"?

#### Scale flips the bottleneck from talent to capital — and splits Musk and Altman

**Karen Hao:** It's so interesting, because at the time the idea that you needed a lot of compute was actually neither very popular nor seen as that scientifically rigorous. There were many different ideas of how to advance AI. One was: we already have all the techniques we need, we just need to scale them. But that was considered a very extreme opinion. And on the other extreme it was: we don't even have the techniques yet. And interestingly, recently there's a New York Times story that says "Why we likely won't get to AGI anytime soon," by [Cade Metz](https://www.nytimes.com/by/cade-metz), and he cites this stat that 75% of the longest-standing, most respected AI researchers actually still think to this day we don't have the techniques to get to AGI, if we ever will. So we're kind of coming full circle now, and it's starting to become unpopular again, this idea that you can just scale your way to so-called intelligence. But that was the research vibe when OpenAI started: we can actually maybe just innovate on techniques.

::: {.callout-note}
**Editor's note.** The Cade Metz story drew on a March 2025 [Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence](https://aaai.org/) (AAAI) presidential panel report in which about 76% of the surveyed researchers said scaling up current approaches was unlikely to produce AGI — close to Hao's "75%," though the exact wording is about scaling rather than "having the techniques."
:::

**Karen Hao:** And then very quickly — because Ilya Sutskever in particular was a scientist who anomalously did think that scaling was possible, and because Altman loved the idea of adding zeros to things from his career in Silicon Valley, and because [Greg Brockman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greg_Brockman), the chief technology officer, also a very Silicon Valley entrepreneur, liked that idea as well — then they identified, why don't we go for scale, because that's going to be the fastest way to see whether we can beat Google.

And once they made that decision, about less than a year in, roughly, is when they decided we actually need to convert into a for-profit, because the bottleneck has shifted now from acquiring talent to acquiring capital.

And that is also why Elon Musk and Sam Altman ended up having a falling-out, because when they started discussing a for-profit conversion, both Musk and Altman each wanted to be the CEO of that for-profit. And so they couldn't agree.

And originally Ilya Sutskever and Greg Brockman chose Musk — they thought Musk would be the better leader of OpenAI. But then Altman essentially — and this is a very classic pattern in his career — became very persuasive to Brockman, who he'd had a long-term relationship with, about why it could actually be dangerous to go with Musk, and "I would definitely be the more responsible leader," so on and so forth.

And then Brockman convinces Sutskever, and the two — chief scientist, chief technology officer — pivot their decision and go with Altman. And then Musk leaves in a huff and says, "I don't want to be part of this anymore" — which has become rather typical of the man, hasn't it, subsequently.

#### What "open" meant, and how fast it shifted

**Aaron Bastani:** But that is incredible, really. So by 2016 there's a recognition that in terms of capital investment they're going to have to go toe-to-toe with maybe, at that point, the world's biggest company — and they're a nonprofit.

**Karen Hao:** Yeah.

**Aaron Bastani:** I just find it weird that — and lots of people bought the propaganda that OpenAI was in some way open. What did the "open" stand for, by the way?

**Karen Hao:** The "open" originally stood for open source, which in the first year of OpenAI they really did — they did research, and then they would put all their code online. So it really was like they did what they said. And then the moment that they realized "we've got to go for scale," then everything shifted.

**Aaron Bastani:** It's such an amazing story, and so emblematic of the 2010s, that you have this organization which presents itself as effectively an extension of activism — and ends up becoming today, some people value OpenAI at $300 billion. And it's doing all these terrible things which we're going to talk about.

### [0:32:50 — Who is Sam Altman?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8enXRDlWguU&t=1970s) {#ch-sam-altman}

#### From Loopt to YC president: a networker, not an operator

**Aaron Bastani:** Sam Altman specifically — who is he? What's his background? How does this guy who nobody's heard of become the CEO of a company which today is almost more valuable than any company in Europe, for instance?

**Karen Hao:** Altman has spent his entire career in Silicon Valley. He was first a startup founder himself, and he was part of the first batch of companies that joined Y Combinator — now one of the most prestigious startup accelerators in Silicon Valley, but at the time he was the very first class and no one really knew what YC was. He did that for seven years.

He was running a company called [Loopt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loopt), a mobile-based social media platform, effectively a Foursquare competitor — but which actually started earlier than Foursquare. It didn't do very well. It was sold off for parts. But what he did do very well during that time was ingratiate himself with very powerful networks in Silicon Valley.

So one of the first and longest mentors he ended up having throughout his career is [Paul Graham](https://www.paulgraham.com/), the founder of Y Combinator, who then plucked Sam Altman to be his successor. And Altman then, at a very young age, became president of YC, and ended up doing that for around 5 years.

During his tenure at YC, he dramatically expanded YC's portfolio of companies — he started investing not just in software companies but also pushing into quantum, into self-driving cars, into fusion, really going for those hard-tech engineering challenges.

And if you look at how he ended up then as CEO of OpenAI, I think he basically was trying to figure out what's going to be the next big technology wave: let me test out all of these different things, position myself as involved in all of these different things.

So in addition to all his investments, he started cultivating this idea of, AI also seems like maybe it'll be big — let me start working on an idea for a fundamental AI research lab that becomes OpenAI. And once OpenAI started being the fastest one taking off, then Altman hops over and becomes CEO.

#### How he became CEO when Ilya and Brockman ran the company

**Aaron Bastani:** He hops over. So how does that happen? Where does he come from? Because, like you say, originally — who's there first, him or Ilya?

**Karen Hao:** Technically Altman recruited Sutskever, but Altman was only a chairman — he didn't take an executive role at OpenAI, even though he founded the company. And similarly with Musk: Musk didn't have an executive role, he was just a co-chairman. So it was just the two of them that were chairmen of the board, and Ilya Sutskever and Greg Brockman were the main executives actually running the company day-to-day in the beginning.

**Aaron Bastani:** I have to say, reading the book, Sam Altman comes across as a masterful manipulator and understander of human psychology.

There's this great quote — let me get it up — which you have, I think it's from Paul Graham: "Sam Altman — you could parachute him into an island full of cannibals and come back in 5 years and he'd be the king." "If you're Sam Altman, you don't have to be profitable to convey to investors that you will succeed with or without them." He's also described, by the way, as a "once-in-a-generation fundraising talent" — I think that's by you.

How is he able to just basically come out of nowhere and compete with people like Elon Musk, Zuckerberg, as this kind of intellectual heavyweight in Silicon Valley in regards to one of the major growth technologies of our decade?

**Karen Hao:** So from the public's perspective, he came out of nowhere. But within the tech industry, everyone knew Sam Altman. I, as someone who worked in tech, knew Sam Altman ages ago, because Y Combinator was just so important.

**Aaron Bastani:** As a CEO of a potential company that valuable — was it always something that he might be in?

**Karen Hao:** No, I don't think people ever thought that he would jump to become the CEO of a company, because he has such an investor mindset, and his approach has always been to be involved in many, many companies. He invested in hundreds of startups, as both president of YC and running some personal investment funds as well. But people — he was well respected within the valley. He was seen as a critical linchpin of the entire startup ecosystem.

And not just by people within the industry, but by policymakers, which is key. He started cultivating relationships with politicians very early on in his tenure as president of YC. For example, I talk in my book about how [Ash Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ash_Carter), the head of the Department of Defense under the Obama administration, came to Altman asking, "How can we get more young tech entrepreneurs to partner with the US government?" So he was seen as a gateway into the valley.

And obviously the valley isn't just made of startups, there's also the tech giants. But back then, starting a startup was way cooler than working at a tech giant, because Google, Microsoft were considered the older, safer options if you really wanted job security. But if you wanted to be an innovator, if you wanted to do breathtaking things, you would build a startup. And your number one goal as a startup founder was to get into YC. So Altman was the pinnacle — he was emblematic of the pinnacle of success in the valley.

**Aaron Bastani:** And even if his net worth wasn't the same as other people, in terms of his social capital, his networking, he understood early on that's where the real value lies.

**Karen Hao:** Exactly.

#### "I don't know what Sam believes"

**Aaron Bastani:** So interesting. Some notes that I wrote down — because there are points where I'm thinking, why on earth is this gentleman the CEO of such a valuable company, he seems kind of useless — the notes I had down were: people-pleaser, yes-liar. At points it comes across as almost psychotic, the capacity to lie.

Here's an interesting question for me, and I don't know how comfortable you are with answering it. In writing this book, there's another alternative timeline where you basically write a hagiography of Sam and you leave all of that out, right?

There are other writers out there — I won't name them — they sell a ton of books, and they write very positive, affirming biographies of these visionary leaders, whether it's Elon Musk or Steve Jobs etc. Why didn't you just write that book about Sam Altman? You would have made a ton more money.

I'm reading this stuff and I'm thinking, my goodness, this is so deft and nuanced, your portrait of Sam Altman — I just think, this is going to really hurt him when he reads this stuff, I imagine. Why didn't you take the easy route?

**Karen Hao:** I don't know that that would have been the easy route. I just wrote the facts, and the facts come out that way. I interviewed over 260 people across 300 different interviews, and over 150 of those interviews were with people who either worked at the company or were close to Sam Altman. And that's just what they presented — all of the details that I ended up putting in.

And one of the things that came through again and again — well, two things. No matter how long someone worked with him or how closely, they would always say to me, "At the end of the day, I don't know what Sam believes."

**Aaron Bastani:** That's interesting.

**Karen Hao:** And then the other thing that came through was, I would ask them, "Well, what did he say to you he believed in this meeting, at this point in time, for why the company needed to do this XYZ thing?" And the answer was, he always said he believed what that person believed. Except, because I interviewed so many people who have very divergent beliefs, I was like, wait a minute, he's saying that he believes what this person believes, and then what that person believes, and they're literally diametrically opposite.

So I just ended up documenting all of those different details to illustrate how people feel about him. He's a polarizing figure, both extreme in the positive and negative direction. Some people feel he is the greatest tech leader of our generation — but they don't say that he is honest when they say that. They just say that he's one of the most phenomenal assets for achieving a vision of the future that they really agree with.

And then there are other people who hate his guts and say that he is the greatest threat ever. And it really comes down to whether or not they agree with his vision. And if they don't, then his persuasive powers suddenly become manipulative tactics.

#### Comparative advantage: psychology, persuasion, the one-on-one

**Aaron Bastani:** If you compare him to somebody like Elon Musk as a CEO, who is obviously far from perfect — but Elon Musk makes big bets, he has gut instincts, he's very happy to alienate people if he thinks he's right about something. And obviously I don't agree with him on many things, but there's an archetype with regards to a business leader that looks like that.

And then you've got somebody like Sam Altman — he's doing all of these things, the people-pleasing, the conflict-aversion, and yet he's managed to lead this company to essentially a third-of-a-trillion valuation. He must obviously be doing something right as well. So what are his comparative advantages as a business leader?

Because on paper I read all that stuff and I think the guy wouldn't be able to get up in the morning and make breakfast, and yet he's accomplished some extraordinary things.

**Karen Hao:** Yeah, I think it really comes down to — he does understand human psychology very well, which is helpful in getting people to join in on his quest. So he's great at acquiring talent. And he's said himself, "I'm a visionary leader, I'm not an operational leader, and my best skill is to acquire the best people that then operationalize the thing." So he's good at persuading people into joining his quest.

He's good at persuading whoever has access to whatever resource he needs to then give him that resource — whether it's capital, land, energy, water, laws. And people have said that he instills a very powerful sense of belief, in his vision and in their ability to then do it.

**Aaron Bastani:** We say in English soccer, we'd say "good man-manager." He can inspire people.

**Karen Hao:** He inspires people to do things that they didn't think they would be able to do. But yeah — this is why there's so much controversy. Everyone has a very personalized relationship with him, because he does his best work in one-on-one meetings, when he can say whatever he needs to say to get you to believe or achieve whatever it is that he needs you to do.

And that's also part of the reason why there's so many diverging accounts — people who are like, "Oh, I think he believes this, I think he believes that," and they're totally diverging. It's because he's having these very personalized conversations with people.

So some people end up coming out of those meetings feeling totally transformed in the positive direction, being like, "I feel superhuman, I can now do all these things, and it's in the direction that I want to go — I'm building the future that he sees and I see, and we're aligned." And then other people end up coming out of these meetings feeling like, "Was I played? Was he just telling me all these things to get me to do something that's actually fundamentally against my values?"

**Aaron Bastani:** You said you spoke to 150 people who were connected with OpenAI — over 150 interviews.

**Karen Hao:** Yeah. Sorry — 150 interviews, 250 interviews altogether, 270 people altogether. The numbers were—

**Aaron Bastani:** No, but it's absolutely incredible.

::: {.callout-note}
**Editor's note.** The interview counts get muddled here on the fly. As the intro voiceover and the book itself state, *Empire of AI* draws on more than 300 interviews with around 260 people, including roughly 150 interviews with about 90 current and former OpenAI employees.
:::

### [0:45:40 — Who is Karen Hao?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8enXRDlWguU&t=2740s) {#ch-karen-hao}

#### From MIT mechanical engineering to AI journalism

**Aaron Bastani:** I should have said this right at the start, really. What's your personal bio on all this stuff? Because of course, when people out of journalism, media cover technology — the intersection of that with politics — we go, "Well, they don't really know what they're talking about, they're generalists, because they come out of journalism." What's your background? Because it's quite particular.

**Karen Hao:** I studied mechanical engineering at MIT for undergrad, and I went and worked in Silicon Valley, because that's what I thought I wanted to do. I lasted a year before I realized it was absolutely not what I wanted to do. And then I went into journalism.

And the reason I had such a visceral reaction against Silicon Valley is because I was quite interested in sustainability and how to mitigate climate change. The reason I went to study engineering in the first place was, I thought that technology could be a great tool for social change, and for shaping consumer behaviors to prevent us from planetary disaster. And I realized that Silicon Valley's incentive structures for producing technology were not actually leading us to develop technologies in the public interest. In fact, most often it was leading to technologies that were eroding the public interest.

And the problems like mitigation of climate change that I was interested in were not profitable problems. But that is ultimately what Silicon Valley builds — they want to build profitable technologies. And so it just seemed to me that it didn't really make sense to try and continue doing what I wanted to do within a structure that didn't reward that.

And then I thought, well, I've always liked writing, maybe I can use writing as a tool for social change. So I switched to journalism.

**Aaron Bastani:** You went to MIT Review, right?

**Karen Hao:** And then I went to a few publications, and then eventually MIT Technology Review, to cover AI, and then Wall Street Journal.

**Aaron Bastani:** And then the Wall Street Journal. These are big — just so people know, there's real credibility behind this, all these interviews, this CV. And it's interesting as well — you say, "I wouldn't write a hagiography, I just wrote what was there." Maybe that's partly an extension of your STEM background, right? Rather than writing propaganda or a puff piece, which let's be honest is most coverage of the sector. But it's true, right?

#### Why the engineering degree helps: "I don't find there to be magic"

**Karen Hao:** Well, people often ask me, "How much did my engineering degree help me in reporting on this?" And I think it helps me in ways that are not what people would typically assume. I went to school with a lot of the people that now build these technologies. I went to school with some of the executives at OpenAI. And so for me, I do not find there to be magic. I don't find these figures to be towering or magical. Like, I remember when we were walking around dorm rooms together in our pajamas, and it instilled in me this understanding that technology is always a product of human choices.

And different humans will have different blind spots. And if you give a small group of those people too much power to develop technologies that will affect billions of people's lives, inevitably that is structurally unsound. We should not be allowing small groups of individuals to concentrate such profound influence on society, when you cannot expect any individual to have such great visibility into everything that's happening in the world and perfectly understand how to craft a one-size-fits-all technology that ends up being profoundly beneficial for everyone. It just doesn't make sense at all.

And I think the other thing it really helps me with is — Silicon Valley is an extremely elitist place, and it allows me to have an honest conversation with people faster.

Because if they start stonewalling me, or trying to pretend that there are certain things these technologies are capable of that they're not actually capable of, I will just slap my MIT degree down and be like, "Cut the bullcrap, tell me what's actually happening." And it is a shortcut to getting them to speak more honestly to me.

But it's not actually because of what I studied. It's more just that it signals to them that they need to speed up their throat-clearing.

#### Is this an existential challenge to democracy?

**Aaron Bastani:** That's really interesting, though. Because I do feel like lots of coverage of this sector — I can only speak in regards to the UK, and we're a tiddler compared to you guys — but at the intersection of particularly politics and technology, the coverage by political journalists at Westminster... Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves say, "We're going to build more data centers, isn't that fantastic?" Actually, not necessarily — they're not going to create that many jobs once they're built, they can use a ton of energy, a ton of water. What's the upside for the UK taxpayer? There is very little interrogation of just the press releases.

And it's really interesting to me that you've come out of MIT and then taken this trajectory. Is this stuff you just talked about — knowing these people, this tiny group of people whose decisions now affect billions already — is it, on the present trajectory, an existential challenge to democracy? And "challenge" is speculative — is it going to end democracy?

**Karen Hao:** I think it is greatly threatening and increasing the likelihood of democracy's demise. But I never make predictions of "this outcome will happen," because it makes it sound inevitable.

And one of the reasons I wrote the book is because I very much believe that we can change that, and people can act now to shape the future so that we don't lose democracy.

But on this trajectory — if the next 20 years are like the last 20 years — on this trajectory, for sure, I think it will end democracy.

**Aaron Bastani:** We've really screwed up in the last 20 years, right? I wonder — gosh.

**Karen Hao:** Yeah. I'll give it maybe 20 years.

**Aaron Bastani:** 20 years. Yeah. We used to have this thing called privacy, high streets, childhood — all gone.

### [0:51:49 — Colonial similarities to AI companies](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8enXRDlWguU&t=3109s) {#ch-colonial}

#### Why OpenAI's true resource use is unknowable

**Aaron Bastani:** You've said that what OpenAI did in the last few years is they started blowing up the amount of data and the size of the computers needed to do this training, in regards to the deep learning. Give me a sense of the scale. We've talked a little bit about the data centers, but how much energy, land, water is being used to power OpenAI, just specifically as one company?

**Karen Hao:** To power OpenAI — that's really hard, because they don't actually tell us this. We only have figures for the industry at large and the amount of data centers.

**Aaron Bastani:** So it's not in their annual reports, for instance.

**Karen Hao:** No. Well, they don't have annual reports, because they're not a public company.

**Aaron Bastani:** Of course.

**Karen Hao:** And actually it doesn't matter if they're a public company, because Google and Microsoft do have annual reports, where they say how much capital they've spent on data center construction. They do not break down how much of those data centers are being used for AI.

They also have sustainability reports, where they talk about the water and carbon and things like that, but they do not break down how much of that is coming from AI either. And they also massage that data a lot to make it seem better than it actually is.

But even with the massaging, there was that story — last year, 2024 — where both Google and Microsoft reported, I think it was a 30% and 50% jump in their carbon emissions, largely driven by this data center development.

::: {.callout-note}
**Editor's note.** Both companies report emissions against different baselines: Microsoft's 2024 sustainability report put its total emissions up roughly 30% since its 2020 baseline, and Google reported its emissions up about 48% since 2019 — both attributing much of the rise to data center electricity demand and construction.
:::

**Aaron Bastani:** And also the context here is, over the last — it was one of the good-news stories of the last 10 to 15 years — that CO₂ emissions per capita in the US has kind of plateaued, right? Across the West it had kind of plateaued, and actually in the UK energy consumption dropped — I mean, we stopped making things, but still, everything's made in East Asia now.

But it was kind of a good story, and I kind of bought it. I thought that we'd kind of plateaued — obviously the Global South would consume more energy, but we are as well.

Should we look at these companies as kind of analogous to the [East India Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company) of the 19th century?

#### The East India Company analogy

**Karen Hao:** That is the analogy that I have increasingly started using, especially with the Trump administration in power, because the British East India Company very much was a corporate empire, and started off not very imperial. They just started off as a company, a very small company based in London. And of course, through economic trade agreements with India, gained significant economic power, political power, and eventually became the apex predator in that ecosystem — and that's when they started being very imperial in nature.

And they were, the entire time, abetted by the British Empire, the nation-state empire. So you have a corporate empire, you have a nation-state empire, and I literally see that dynamic playing out now, where the US government is also in its empire era. The Trump administration has quite literally used words to suggest that he wants to expand and fortify the American empire, and he sees these corporate empires like OpenAI as his empire-building assets.

And so I think he is probably seeing it in the same way that the British crown saw the British East India Company: let's just let this company acquire all these resources, do all these things, and then eventually we'll nationalize the company — and then India formally becomes a colony of the British Empire.

So whatever the modern-day equivalent would be of nationalizing these companies is Trump's endgame. He is helping them strike all these deals and installing all this American hardware and software all around the world, with the hope that then those become national assets.

And there was actually just a recent op-ed in the Financial Times from [Marietje Schaake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marietje_Schaake), one of the former EU parliamentarians, who pointed out: isn't it so convenient for the US to get all of this American infrastructure installed everywhere around the world, so that the US government could literally turn it off at any time?

If you want to talk about empire-building, there's that. But at the same time, these corporate empires are also trying to use the American empire as an asset to their empire-building ambitions. So there's a very tenuous alliance between Silicon Valley and Washington right now, in that each one is trying to use the other, and ultimately trying to dominate the other.

And there's a growing popularity in Silicon Valley of this idea of a "politics of exit" — this idea that democracy doesn't work anymore, we need to find other ways of organizing ourselves in society, and maybe the best way is actually a series of networked companies with CEOs at the top.

So I don't ultimately know who's going to win — the nation-state empire or the corporate empire. But either version is bad, because all of the people in power now, both the business executives and the politicians, do not actually care at all about preserving democracy.

#### 1857, and the violence behind the company

**Aaron Bastani:** The analogy of India is really interesting. So — I think I might have my dates wrong — the East India Company is running things until 1857. You have the Indian Mutiny, basically an uprising against the East India Company, and then of course that commercial endeavor has to be underpinned by the organized violence of the British imperial state. And it does feel like that could be the next step of what happens with regards to US interests overseas.

I suppose one retort would be, "Well, hold on, it sounds kind of good." I'm a socialist. I kind of like the idea of SpaceX being nationalized. I kind of like the idea of the federal government having a 51% stake in OpenAI and Tesla and Meta. What would you say to that?

**Karen Hao:** I don't necessarily know if my critique is of the nationalization of the company, more as: why are they nationalizing these companies? Because of this endgame mentality of "let's just let these companies run rampant around the world, so that ultimately whatever their assets are become our assets," it is leading the Trump administration to have a completely hands-off approach to AI regulation.

They quite literally proposed the [big, beautiful bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Big_Beautiful_Bill_Act), which passed the House and is now going up to the Senate, with a clause that would, if implemented, put a 10-year moratorium on AI regulation at the state level — which is usually where sensible regulation happens in the US.

So they're doing all of these actions now with wide-ranging repercussions that will be very difficult to unwind, in the name of this idea that maybe if they just allow these companies to act with total impunity, it will ultimately benefit the nation-state.

::: {.callout-note}
**Editor's note.** The 10-year moratorium on state AI laws passed the House as part of the bill in May 2025; the Senate stripped the provision out at the start of July 2025 in a near-unanimous vote, so the moratorium did not become law.
:::

#### Territories as resources: rural US and UK communities

**Aaron Bastani:** How do people like Sam Altman look at the rest of the world outside the US? These kind of tech leaders — how do they look at Little Britain and Italy, how do they look at us? What do they think about us? You've been inside their minds.

**Karen Hao:** Yeah. They see them as resources. They see different territories as different types of resources — which is what older empires did. They would look at a map and just draw out the resources that they could acquire in each geography. We're going to go here and acquire the labor, we're going to go here and acquire the land, we're going to go here and acquire the minerals. That's literally how they talk.

When I was talking with some OpenAI researchers about their data center expansion, there was this one OpenAI employee who said, "We're running out of land and water." And he was just saying, "Yeah, we're just trying to look at the whole world and see where else we can place these things. What other geographies can we find all the conditions that we need to build more data centers — land without earthquakes, without floods, without tornadoes, hurricanes, all these natural disasters, and can deliver massive amounts of energy to a single point, and can cool the systems?"

And they're looking at that level of abstraction: what are the different pieces of territory and resources that we need to acquire? And that includes other parts of the West.

**Aaron Bastani:** That's not just the Global South.

**Karen Hao:** No, it includes other parts of the West as well. So there have been rapid data center expansions in rural communities in both the US and the UK, and they always end up in economically vulnerable communities, because those are the communities that often actually opt in to the data center development initially, because they are not informed about what it will ultimately cost them, and for how long.

I spoke with this one Arizona legislator who said, "I didn't know it had to use fresh water." And for the UK audience, Arizona is a desert territory — there's a very, very stringent budget on freshwater. And after that legislator found out, she was like, "I would have never voted for having this data center in."

But the problem is that there are so few independent experts for these legislators, city council members to consult, that the only people they rely on for information about what the impact is going to be are the companies. And all the companies ever say is, "We're going to invest millions of dollars, we're going to create a bunch of construction jobs up front, and it's going to be great for your economy."

**Aaron Bastani:** That's all we hear about data centers in this country. And it's a great top line for the chancellor and the prime minister, because they can say "tens of billions of pounds worth of investment." But in terms of long-term jobs, how many?

And also, by the way, for that rural community in God-knows-where, the northeast of England or whatever — you're not telling them that actually they can't use their hose pipes for 3 months a year because all the water is going to that local data center.

**Karen Hao:** Exactly.

#### The M4 housing ban and the "false trade-off" of scale

**Aaron Bastani:** And it's quite extraordinary — and the most scary thing about all of it is, in the UK at least, the politicians don't know any of that. I sincerely don't think the chancellor knows any of that.

And even if you use the prism of colonialism, imperialism with regards to exploitative economic relations between the United States and other parts of the world, they think you're a Trotskyist, right? That's the crazy thing. They can't even look after their own people, because if looking after your own people boils down to being too left-wing—

**Karen Hao:** Well, I think part of it is also that they don't really realize that it's literally happening in the UK. So to connect it to the UK: data center development along the M4 corridor has literally already led to a ban on construction of new housing in certain communities that desperately need more affordable housing.

And it's because you cannot build new housing when you cannot guarantee deliveries of fresh water or electricity to that housing. And it was due to the massive electricity consumption of the data centers being built in that corridor that led to that ban.

**Aaron Bastani:** That's nuts. That's the most valuable real estate for housing in the country, the M4.

**Karen Hao:** Yeah.

**Aaron Bastani:** And do you think UK politicians are aware of that contradiction?

**Karen Hao:** I don't know if they are aware. Maybe they don't have awareness, or maybe they are aware and they're also thinking of other trade-offs.

Now in the UK and the EU at large, there's just this huge conversation around data sovereignty, and of course technology sovereignty — there's this whole concept of developing the "EU stack," and why is it that we don't have any of our own tech giants, why don't we have any of this infrastructure? And here, Starmer just said this week, during London Tech Week, "We want to be AI creators, not AI consumers."

So I think in their minds, maybe this is a viable trade-off: we skimp a little bit on housing for the ability to have more indigenous innovation.

But I think the thing that is often left out of that conversation is, this is a false trade-off. People think that you need colossal data centers to build AI systems. You actually do not.

This is specifically the approach that OpenAI decided to take. But actually, before OpenAI started building large language models and generative AI systems at these colossal scales, the trend within the AI research community was going the opposite direction, towards tiny AI systems. And there was all this really interesting research looking into how small your data sets could be to create powerful AI models, and how little computational resources you needed.

There were interesting papers I wrote about, where you could have a couple hundred images to create highly performant AI systems, or you could have AI systems trained on your mobile device — running on a single computer chip on your mobile device. And OpenAI took an approach that is now using hundreds of thousands of computer chips to train a single system. And those hundreds of thousands of computer chips now are consuming city-loads of energy.

So if we divorced the concept of AI progress from this scaling paradigm, you would realize that you can have housing and you can have AI innovation. But once again, there's not a lot of independent experts that are actually saying these things. Most AI experts today are employed by these companies. And this is basically the equivalent of if most climate scientists were being bankrolled by oil and gas companies. They would tell you things that are not in any sense of the word scientifically grounded, but just good for the company.

**Aaron Bastani:** I interviewed a great guy — twice, actually, now — a guy called Angus Hanton, who's really just on it with regards to the increasingly exploitative nature of the United States' economic relations with the UK. Just fascinating — a book and a man. And I just don't think it's cut through to our politicians here how bad it's getting.

And you're saying about AI consumers or creators — I mean, ultimately, you're talking about Meta, you're talking about Alphabet, you're talking about xAI, you're talking about OpenAI — we are consumers, we are dependent. It's a colonial, exploitative relationship with regards to big tech, has been for a really long time.

Our smartest people, who the taxpayer trains here, go to the US. I think one of the top people — Demis [Hassabis], a UK national, you know — DeepMind, now working under the umbrella of Alphabet. And it just doesn't make sense to me — they simply don't get it.

I came here using my Mastercard; millions of Brits use Apple Pay and Google Pay and Mastercard and Visa, and every time we do, 0.1, 0.2% crosses the Atlantic. And it just goes over the heads of our political class, which is very unnerving — in regards to the efficiency of these smaller systems. Where does DeepSeek fit in all of this?

### [1:07:39 — DeepSeek](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8enXRDlWguU&t=4059s) {#ch-deepseek}

#### What DeepSeek showed: frontier capability at a fraction of the compute

**Aaron Bastani:** Because of course the scaling laws at the heart of OpenAI — which is, you get to AGI by more compute, more parameters, more data — are kind of untethered a bit by the arrival of [DeepSeek](https://www.deepseek.com/).

**Karen Hao:** Yes.

**Aaron Bastani:** What?

**Karen Hao:** DeepSeek is such an interesting and complicated case, because it's a Chinese AI model that was created by this company [High-Flyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High-Flyer), and they were able to create a model that essentially matched and even exceeded some performance metrics of American models being developed by OpenAI and Anthropic, with orders of magnitude less computational resources, less money. That said, it's not necessarily the perfect — I don't think the world should suddenly start using DeepSeek and saying DeepSeek solves all these problems, because it's still engaged in a lot of data privacy problems, copyright exploitation, things like that.

And some people argue that ultimately they were distilling the models that were first developed through the scaling paradigm. So you first develop some of these colossal scaling models, and then you end up making them smaller and more efficient. So some people argue that you actually have to first do that scaling before you get the efficiency.

But anyway, what it did show is you can get these capabilities with significantly less compute. And it also showed a complete unwillingness of American companies — now that they know they can use these techniques to make their models more efficient, they're still not really doing it.

::: {.callout-note}
**Editor's note.** DeepSeek reported that the final training run for its V3 model (671 billion total parameters, 37 billion active per token) cost about $5.6 million in compute — orders of magnitude below the figures associated with comparable US models. That number is the headline final-run cost only; it excludes prior research, failed runs, and the cost of the GPU cluster itself, which is why "$5.6M built DeepSeek" is often called misleading.
:::

#### Why US labs won't economize: monopoly logic and path dependence

**Aaron Bastani:** Why? Do they like giving their money to Nvidia?

**Karen Hao:** Because when you continue to pursue a scaling approach, and you're the only one with all of the AI experts in the world, you persuade people into believing this is the only path, and therefore you continue to monopolize this technology, because it locks out anyone else from playing that game.

And also because of path dependence — these companies are actually not that nimble. It's not so easy for them to just immediately swap to a different approach.

They end up putting in motion all the resources, all of the training runs, so on and so forth, over the course of months, and then they just have to run with it.

#### The Stable Diffusion precedent — and Jensen Huang's charisma

**Karen Hao:** So DeepSeek actually wasn't the first time this happened. The first time was with image generators and [Stable Diffusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stable_Diffusion). And Stable Diffusion was specifically developed by an academic in Europe who was really pissed that the AI companies like OpenAI were taking a scaling approach to image generation.

He was like, this is literally wholly unnecessary. And they're spending thousands of chips, all of this energy, to produce [DALL·E](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DALL-E). And ultimately, he ended up producing Stable Diffusion with a couple hundred chips, using a new technique called [latent diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.10752) [[1]](#ref-1), hence the name Stable Diffusion.

And arguably it was actually an even better model than DALL·E, because users were saying that Stable Diffusion had even better image quality, better image generation, better ability to actually control the images than DALL·E.

But even knowing that latent diffusion existed, OpenAI continued to develop DALL·E with these massive scaling approaches. And it wasn't until later that they adopted the cheaper version. But it was significantly delayed. And I was asking OpenAI researchers, like, why? That doesn't make any sense, why did you do that? And they were like, well, once you set off on a path, it's kind of hard to pivot.

Also, [Jensen Huang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jensen_Huang), the CEO of Nvidia, is really charismatic, right? It's quite funny, because — I'm a Marxist, I'm going to make that confession — you have these big structural understandings of how history happens, and then you sort of realize, actually, this guy's really charismatic, and this person's really manipulative, and all of a sudden the world's hyperpower is making these technological decisions. Quite strange.

### [1:11:49 — Exploitative practices in the Global South](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8enXRDlWguU&t=4309s) {#ch-global-south}

#### Kenya: building OpenAI's content-moderation filter

**Aaron Bastani:** We talked about data centers, we talked about earth, water, energy. I want to talk also about some of the more exploitative practices with regards to workers in the Global South. You use one really grueling example, actually, in Kenya. Can you talk about some of the research around that, some of the people you met?

**Karen Hao:** Yeah. So I ended up interviewing workers in Kenya who were contracted by OpenAI to build a content moderation filter for the company. And at that point in the company's history, it was starting to think about commercialization, after coming from its nonprofit fundamental-AI-research roots. And they realized, if we're going to put a text generation model in the hands of millions of users, it's going to be a PR crisis if it starts spewing racist, toxic, hateful speech.

In fact, in 2016, Microsoft infamously did exactly this. They developed a chatbot named [Tay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tay_(chatbot)). They put it online without any content moderation, and then within hours it started saying awful things, and they had to take it offline. And to this day — as evidenced by me bringing it up — it's still brought up as a horrible case study in corporate mismanagement.

And so OpenAI thought, we don't want to do that, we're going to create a filter that wraps around our models, so that even if the models start generating this stuff, it never reaches the user, because the filter blocks it.

In order to build that filter, what the Kenyan workers had to do was wade through reams of the worst text on the internet, as well as AI-generated text where OpenAI was prompting its models to imagine the worst text on the internet. And the workers then had to go through all of this and put it into a detailed taxonomy: is this hate speech, is this harassment, is this violent content, is this sexual content? And the degree of hate speech, of violence, of sexual content. So they were asking workers to say, does it involve sexual abuse? Does it involve sexual abuse of children? So on and so forth.

And to this day, I believe if you look at OpenAI's content moderation filter documentation, it actually lists all of those categories. And this is one of the things that it offers to business clients of their models — that you can toggle on and off each of these filters. So that's why they had to put this into that taxonomy.

#### Mophat: when the trauma breaks a family

**Karen Hao:** The workers ended up suffering very many of the same symptoms as content moderators of the social media era. Absolutely traumatized by the work, completely changed their personalities, left them with PTSD [post-traumatic stress disorder]. And I highlight the story of this man Mophat, one of the workers I interviewed, who showed to me that it's not just individuals that break down — it's their families and communities, because there are people who rely on these individuals.

Mophat was on the sexual content team. His personality totally changed as he was reading child sexual abuse every day. And when he came home, he stopped playing with his stepdaughter, he stopped being intimate with his wife.

And he also couldn't explain to them why he was changing, because he didn't know how to say to them, "I read sex content all day." That doesn't sound like a real job — it sounds like a very shameful job. ChatGPT hadn't come out yet, so there was no conception of what that even meant.

And so one day, his wife asks him for fish for dinner. He goes out, buys three fish — one for him, one for her, one for the stepdaughter — and by the time he comes home, all of their bags are packed and they're completely gone. And she texts him, "I don't know the man you've become anymore, and I'm never coming back."

#### Images, the Sama scandal, and a few dollars an hour
